name: No World Order
editorial_article:
Released in 1993, 'No World Order' stands as a landmark experimental work by American multi-instrumentalist and producer Todd Rundgren, recorded under his alias TR-i. It holds a distinct place in music history as the first truly interactive album. Developed specifically for the Philips CD-i multimedia platform, the project was designed to shatter the static nature of recorded music by allowing the listener to manipulate playback in real-time. By utilizing an interface that controlled tempo, mood, mix complexity, and musical form, users could rearrange segments of the music—which consisted of over 900 individual four-bar musical cells—to create a personalized experience.

Beyond its technical ambition, the album is a compelling snapshot of Rundgren’s interest in the collision of rock, electronica, and hip-hop. The music itself was crafted to be modular, ensuring that the transitions between user-selected segments remained seamless, regardless of the order in which they were played. While the interactive CD-i version offered the most advanced implementation, Rundgren also released a traditional linear CD version, which served as his curated 'Rundgren mix,' and later, a more conventional song-oriented edition titled 'No World Order Lite'. The project earned accolades from the interactive media community for its pioneering vision of a non-linear musical medium, proving to be years ahead of the algorithmic streaming era that would eventually define how audiences consume music. The 'No World Order' experience remains a testament to Rundgren's long-standing persona as a musical futurist who constantly sought to challenge the boundaries between creator and listener.
editorial_pitch: An ambitious 1993 multimedia experiment by Todd Rundgren (as TR-i), 'No World Order' is recognized as the first interactive album, allowing listeners to rearrange modular musical segments in real-time via the Philips CD-i platform.
